'''''Aesculus californica''''', commonly known as the '''California buckeye''' or '''California horse-chestnut,''' is a species of flowering plant in the soapberry family native primarily to [[California]] and southwestern [[Oregon]]. It is a large shrub or small tree, often with several trunks and a broad, rounded crown. It has palmately compound leaves are among the earliest in spring, followed by erect flower clusters of white to pale pink flowers in late spring and large, pear shapes fruit capsules in late summer.

California buckeye is [[drought deciduous]]: in drier, more inland areas, its leaves commonly fall off and die during late summer, while specimens in moister coastal environments retain their leaves longer into autumn. The large, glossy seeds and other parts of the plant contain toxic [[glycoside]] compounds.

==Description==
''Aesculus californica'' is a large [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]], up to {{cvt|4-12|m|ft}} tall. It typically is multi-trunked, with a crown as broad or broader than it is high. The bark is light gray and smooth.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Anderson |first=Kat |date=30 May 2006 |title=California Buckeye |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/cs_aeca.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com |journal=USDA Plant guide}}</ref> 

The [[Leaf|leaves]] are opposite, and [[Compound leaf|palmately compound]] with five (rarely seven) leaflets. The individual leaflets are {{cvt|6-17|cm}} long, with a finely serrated margin and pointed tips.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Stone |first=William J. |date=24 June 2026 |title=Aesculus californica |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi/auth/challenge?return_to=/eflora/eflora_display.php?name=Aesculus%20californica |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu |publisher=Jepson eFlora}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Aesculus californica {{!}} Landscape Plants {{!}} Oregon State University |url=https://landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/plants/aesculus-californica |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu}}</ref> The leaves are dark green above and paler on the underside and may have downy veins.<ref name=":3" /> 

The [[flower]]s are borne on dense, erect [[panicle]]s {{cvt|15-20|cm|4=0}} long and {{cvt|5-8|cm|4=0}} broad. They are fragrant, white to pale pink, and individual flowers are 1-2.5cm long.<ref name=":3" /> Each flower has a two-lobed [[Calyx (anatomy)|calyx]] 5-8mm long, and 4 sometimes 5 petals. Five to seven stamens project conspicuously beyond the petals.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> This species is [[Andromonoecy|andromonoecious]], with the inflorescences producing both staminate and bisexual flowers on the same plant. Only the bisexual flowers are capable of developing into fruit.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Newell |first=Elizabeth A. |date=1991 |title=Direct and Delayed Costs of Reproduction in Aesculus Californica |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2260719 |journal=Journal of Ecology |publisher=[Wiley, British Ecological Society] |volume=79 |issue=2 |pages=365–378 |doi=10.2307/2260719 |issn=0022-0477|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The [[fruit]] is smoot, leathery pear-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|5-8|cm|4 = 0}} long. As it matures, the capsule turns brown and splits revealing one large, glossy brown [[seed]], measuring {{cvt|2-7|cm|4 = 1}}.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> The seeds are poisonous.<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |isbn=0-394-73127-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/397 397] |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/397 }}</ref> <gallery>
File:Aesculus californica kz1.jpg|Detail of the leaves
File:Aesculus Californica Berkeley2.jpg|A single panicle
File:Aesculus californica Fruit Mount Diablo 9.jpg|Fruit maturing in late summer
File:Aesculus californica drought deciduous Mount Diablo 6.jpg|''A. californica'' with [[Plant senescence|senescent]] leaves in late summer on [[Mount Diablo]]
</gallery>California buckeye has adapted to its native [[Mediterranean climate]] by having an earlier growing season that tracks the availability of moisture. It is among the earliest native woody plants in its range to produce new leaves in spring, and likewise one on the earliest to lose its leaves in late summer. In dry inland populations, the leaves commonly senesce in late spring or summer and are shed as soil moisture evaporates''.'' <ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Callahan |first=Frank |date=2005 |title=California Buckeye |url=https://www.npsoregon.org/kalmiopsis/kalmiopsis12/buckeye.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com |journal=Kalmiopsis |volume=12 |pages=9-15 |issn=1055-419X}}</ref> Those growing in coastal regions tend to hold on to their leaves until mid-autumn.<ref>{{cite book |author=Bakker |first=Elna S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VIIv2O-nF4AC&q=An+Island+Called+California |title=An island called California: an ecological introduction to its natural communities |publisher=University of California Press |year=1984 |isbn=978-0-520-04948-2 |page=74 |access-date=2011-06-11}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
California Buckeye is the only ''Aesculus'' species native to the western United States.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AECA |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref><ref name=Audubon>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-year=1980 |publisher=Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group|isbn=9780394507613 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=540}}</ref> ''A. californica'' is widely distributed in California, growing in the [[Klamath Mountains]] and [[California Coast Ranges]] from  the [[Siskiyou Mountains]] south to [[Los Angeles County, California|Los Angeles County]] and in the  [[Cascade Range]] and lower elevations of the [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]] from [[Shasta County, California|Shasta County]] to [[Kern County, California|Kern County]]. A small, disjunct population occurs near [[Gold Hill, Oregon|Gold Hill]] in the [[Rogue Valley]] in [[Jackson County, Oregon]], separated from the California populations by quite a distance.<ref name=":4" /> 

This species grows in a wide range of conditions: dry slopes, in canyons and along streams generally at low to middle elevations below 1700m.<ref name=":1" /> It occurs as scattered individuals in grasslands as an understory shrub in mixed evergreen forests, and as a component or local dominant of chaparral and oak woodlands.<ref name=":5" /> In the coastal ranges north of Big Sur it is found growing alone on slopes, or intermingled with valley oak (''[[Quercus lobata]]''), Oregon oak (''[[Quercus garryana|Q. garryana]]''), coast live oak (''[[Quercus agrifolia|Q. agrifolia]]'') and California bay laurel (''[[Umbellularia californica]]''). In the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, ''A. californica'' can be found standing alone in grassland at the lowest elevations, intermingled in [[California oak woodland|blue oak woodlands]] at intermediate elevations, and in mixed evergreen forests of black oak (''[[Quercus kelloggii|Q. kelloggii]]''), gray pine (''[[Pinus sabiniana]]''), ponderosa pine (''[[Pinus ponderosa|P. ponderosa]]'') and interior live oak (''[[Quercus wislizeni|Q. wislizeni]]'') as it nears the limit of its range.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CNPS Alliance: Aesculus californica |url=https://vegetation.cnps.org/alliance/12 |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20230825071628/https://vegetation.cnps.org/alliance/12 |archive-date=2023-08-25 |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=vegetation.cnps.org}}</ref>

==Toxicity and uses==
[[File:Aesculus californica-29.jpg|thumb|upright|Seed of the California Buckeye in its husk]]
Native American tribes, including the [[Pomo people|Pomo]], [[Yokuts]], and [[Luiseño people|Luiseño]], used the poisonous nuts and seeds to stupefy schools of fish in small streams to make them easier to catch.<ref>{{cite book |title=A California Flora |author=Philip Alexander Munz |author2=David D. Keck |year=1973 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-02405-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/californiafloras00phil/page/994 994] |url=https://archive.org/details/californiafloras00phil |url-access=registration |quote=buckeye. |access-date=2011-06-20 }}</ref> The bark, leaves, and fruits contain [[neurotoxin|neurotoxic]] [[glycoside]]s, which causes [[hemolysis]] of [[red blood cell]]s.<ref name=":0" /> Buckeye also makes a good fireboard for a [[bow drill]] or hand drill.

Native groups occasionally used the plant as a food supply; after boiling and leaching the toxin out of the seeds or nut meats for several days, they could be ground into a flour or meal similar to that made from acorns.<ref name=Audubon/> The nectar and pollen of the flowers is toxic to [[honeybee]]s,<ref name=Audubon/> so the trees should not be planted near [[Apiary|apiaries]].<ref name=":0">{{cite report |url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_aeca.pdf |title=Plant Guide: California Buckeye, Aesculus californica (Nutt.) Nutt. |author=Anderson |first1=Kat |last2=Roderick |first2=Wayne |date= |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=2025-05-30}}</ref> When the shoots are small and leaves are new, they are lower in toxins and are grazed by livestock and wildlife.<ref name=":5">{{cite report |title=Aesculus californica, in the USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System |author=Howard, Janet L.|publisher=USDA Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/aescal/all.html|access-date=2011-11-07 }}</ref> The flowers are a rich nectar source for many species of butterflies,<ref>{{cite report |url=http://www.mdia.org/Wildlife/wbutterfly.htm |title=Watching Butterflies on Mount Diablo |author=Hintsa |first=Kevin |date= |access-date=2011-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111110102808/http://mdia.org/Wildlife/wbutterfly.htm |archive-date=2011-11-10 |url-status=dead}}</ref> and squirrels and chipmunks consume the seeds.<ref name=Audubon/> [[Hydroquinone]] and [[epicatechin]] have been isolated from the seeds and have been shown to have [[allelopathic]] properties by inhibiting plant growth.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kubo | first1 = Isao | last2 = Matsumoto | first2 = Akiko | last3 = Kozuka | first3 = Mutsuo.  |  last4 = Wood | first4 = William F. | year = 1985 | title = Combined Effect on Plant Growth of (-)-Epicatechin and Hydroquinone, Compounds from Aesculus californica NUTT. (Hippocastanaceae) | journal = Chem. Pharm. Bull. | volume = 33 | issue = 9 | pages = 3826–3828 | doi= 10.1248/cpb.33.3826| doi-access = free }}</ref>

It is used as an ornamental plant for its striking leaf buds, lime green foliage, fragrant white flowers, red-brown foliage in mid to late summer, and architectural silver branches through fall. The tree also acts as a [[Soil stabilization|soil binder]], which prevents [[erosion]] in hilly regions.

==Etymology==
'Aesculus' is [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]]' name for horse chestnuts. It is derived from the old [[Latin|Roman]] name for a different species, ''[[Quercus petraea]]''.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 38, 84</ref>

'Californica' means 'native to [[California]]'.<ref name="gledhill" />
